titleStmt.title: Cognitive Load in Solving Mathematics Problems: Validating the Role of Motivation and the Interaction Among Prior Knowledge, Worked Examples, and Task Difficulty
titleStmt.author: Gupta
Zheng

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Cognitive Load in Solving Mathematics Problems: Validating the Role of Motivation and the Interaction Among Prior Knowledge, Worked Examples, and Task Difficulty

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: It was found that higher-prior knowledge learners performed better with completion-worked examples than full-worked examples whereas lower-prior knowledge learners performed better with full-worked examples than completion-worked examples.

span.label: cognitive load in mathematical problem solving
span.quote: Cognitive load can play a key role in learners’ abilities to solve complex problems like mathematics.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: One hundred and sixty participants were recruited who were randomly assigned into one of eight learning conditions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: When extraneous load is suppressed, working memory resources are freed and become available to the germane and intrinsic load involved in solving the problem
span.quote: In other words, with the influence of extraneous cognitive load abated, the cognitive resources in the working memory become available for the efforts to solve complex mathematics problems that were related to germane (efforts) and intrinsic (content complexity) cognitive load.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: High extraneous load consumes the limited working memory resources, leaving too few for germane load, which is why extraneous load lowers both germane load and the felt probability of success
span.quote: This is further supported by the findings of negative correlation between extraneous cognitive load and probability of success in the current study, suggesting with high extraneous cognitive load the learners would have few cognitive resources left in working memory, hence making little room for germane cognitive load in learning.

span.label: No significant three-way interaction was obtained for cognitive load, which the authors attribute to participants' unfamiliarity with the cognitive-load categories on the self-report questionnaire.
span.note: what this limits: the cognitive-load analysis specifically: THE FAILURE TO OBTAIN A SIGNIFICANT THREE-WAY INTERACTION BY COGNITIVE LOAD INDICATES THAT MORE WORK IS NEEDED
span.quote: The failure to obtain a significant threeway interaction by cognitive load indicates that more work is needed to help learners understand the types of cognitive load when responding to the questionnaire.

span.label: The study is underpowered.
span.note: what this limits: every null in the paper: ANOTHER LIMITATION IS THE POWER OF THE STUDY
span.quote: Another limitation is the power of the study.

span.label: Using the tri-split method to define high- and low-prior-knowledge groups discarded the middle third and may have weakened statistical power; a larger sample is needed.
span.note: what this limits: the prior-knowledge grouping: THE CURRENT STUDY USED THE TRI-SPLIT METHODS IN DEFINING HIGH- AND LOW PRIOR KNOWLEDGE LEARNERS WHICH COULD WEAKEN THE POWER - the middle third is discarded and the groups are constructed
span.quote: More participants may be needed, especially the current study used the tri-split methods in defining high- and lowprior knowledge learners which could weaken the power of the study.

span.label: The construct does not order the outcome it is used to explain, and the paper says so in both directions.
span.note: what this limits: reading a cognitive-load score as a predictor of performance: the paper states high load does not necessarily produce low performance and low load does not guarantee good performance
span.quote: However, high cognitive load does not necessarily end up in low performance and low cognitive load does not mean learners will always perform well in learning.

span.label: The whole construct is measured by asking learners, on a single ten-item self-report instrument.
span.note: what this limits: the cognitive-load values in this study: all three types are scored from one 10-item self-report questionnaire on a 0-10 Likert scale
span.quote: It is a 10-item self-report questionnaire with a Likert scale from 0 (Not at all the case) to 10 (Completely the case). The instrument measures three aspects of cognitive load

span.label: The design compares immediate effects only, and the authors name retention and transfer as what was not examined.
span.note: what this limits: these results as evidence about learning: the study explored immediate effects, with retention and transfer named as future work
span.quote: The current study explored the immediate effects of worked examples in relation to prior knowledge and task difficulty. Future research may examine the long-term effect by inviting participants back after a period of time to study learners’ knowledge retention and transfer.

span.label: a control condition whose learners studied the same problems WITHOUT worked examples, against a group shown half the examples first
span.quote: The learners in control condition studied the problem without worked examples.

span.label: cognitive load
span.quote: Cognitive load can play a key role in learners’ abilities to solve complex problems like mathematics.

span.label: intrinsic cognitive load
span.quote: Intrinsic cognitive load is defined by the difficulty of the instructional materials that cannot be changed or altered.

span.label: extraneous cognitive load
span.quote: Extraneous cognitive load refers to the mental load caused by improper instructional design like imposing redundant information in learning materials that requires learners’ additional processing effort.

span.label: cognitive load - AS MEASURED: three subscales of one ten-item self-report questionnaire, intrinsic on items 1-3, extraneous on 4-6, germane on 7-10
span.quote: The instrument measures three aspects of cognitive load: intrinsic (items 1-3), extraneous (items 4-6), and germane (items 7-10)

span.label: intrinsic cognitive load - defined by the difficulty of the material itself, which the paper says CANNOT be changed or altered
span.quote: Intrinsic cognitive load is defined by the difficulty of the instructional materials that cannot be changed or altered.

span.label: extraneous cognitive load - defined by the instructional design rather than by the material: load caused by improper design such as redundant information
span.quote: Extraneous cognitive load refers to the mental load caused by improper instructional design like imposing redundant information in learning materials that requires learners’ additional processing effort.

span.label: replicates → expertise reversal effect findings of Kalyuga (2007), Kalyuga et al. (1998) and Pollock et al. (2002)
span.quote: Further, the significant main effects for prior knowledge indicated that high- and low-prior knowledge learners differed significantly in intrinsic cognitive load and germane cognitive load when solving complex algebraic problems with different worked examples suggesting an expertise reversal effect, which confirmed the findings in previous research (Kalyuga, 2007; Kalyuga et al., 1998; Pollock et al., 2002).

span.label: builds-on → Sweller, Van Merriënboer and Paas (1998) hypothesis of a negative relationship between extraneous and germane cognitive load
span.quote: A negative correlation between extraneous cognitive load and germane cognitive load (r = -.264, p < .01) was detected which confirms Sweller et al.’s (1998) hypothesis about the negative relationship between extraneous and germane cognitive load.

span.label: intrinsic cognitive load —is-a→ cognitive load
span.quote: Three types of cognitive load exist in learning. They are: intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load.

span.label: extraneous cognitive load —is-a→ cognitive load
span.quote: Three types of cognitive load exist in learning. They are: intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A 2 x 2 x 2 one-way ANOVA was employed to analyze the three-way interaction.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: To address research question 3, the correlation analyses were performed with three types of cognitive load (i.e., intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load) and subcategories of QCM (i.e., anxiety, probability of success, interest, and challenge).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Lower-prior knowledge learners performed better on the posttest with full-worked examples than completion-worked examples (t(1,26) = 1.98, p = .05, 2-tailed).

span.label: Cronbach's alpha
span.quote: The test results were graded by two independent graduate students showing an interrater reliability of Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.993.

span.label: Wilks' Lambda
span.quote: The analysis on the main effect of task difficulty was significant (Wilks’ Lambda λ = .86, p < .05, ŋ2 = .14)

span.label: effect size
span.quote: There was a significant three-way between-subjects effects by posttest (F1, 107 = 4.61, p < .05, ŋ2 = .04) (Figure 2), but no significant three-way interaction for types of cognitive load was detected.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: A family-wise alpha level of .05 was adopted for all analyses with p-values between .05 and .10 labelled as marginal effects and those greater than .10 as not significant.

span.label: biserial correlation
span.quote: The biserial correlations showed a range between 0.22 and 0.64 for easy problems and a range between 0.31 and 0.52 for difficult problems

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Based on the results of pretest, the participants were divided into high, low, and middle prior-knowledge levels with one-standard deviation above the mean as high-prior knowledge (n = 55, m = 10.564, SD = 1.808) and one-standard deviation below the mean as low-prior knowledge (n = 60, m = 3.458, SD = 1.808).

span.label: A significant three-way interaction between prior knowledge, worked example and task difficulty was found on posttest performance, but none was found on any type of cognitive load.
span.quote: There was a significant three-way between-subjects effects by posttest (F1, 107 = 4.61, p < .05, ŋ2 = .04) (Figure 2), but no significant three-way interaction for types of cognitive load was detected.

span.label: Low-prior-knowledge learners scored higher with full-worked examples while high-prior-knowledge learners scored higher with completion-worked examples, an expertise reversal pattern.
span.quote: It was found that lower-prior knowledge learners performed better with full-worked examples than completion-worked examples whereas higher-prior knowledge learners performed better with completion-worked examples than full-worked examples when solving complex math problems.

span.label: Germane cognitive load was significantly positively correlated with learners' interest in the task.
span.quote: The results showed that germane cognitive load was significantly positively correlated with interest (r = .264, p < .01) suggesting the connection between germane cognitive load and learners’ interest in learning.

span.label: Extraneous and germane cognitive load were negatively correlated, confirming the predicted trade-off between them.
span.quote: A negative correlation between extraneous cognitive load and germane cognitive load (r = -.264, p < .01) was detected which confirms Sweller et al.’s (1998) hypothesis about the negative relationship between extraneous and germane cognitive load.

span.label: Task difficulty produced significant differences in intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load but not in germane cognitive load.
span.quote: Significant differences were found between difficult and easy tasks in terms of intrinsic (F = 9.152, p < .001) and extraneous cognitive load (F = 10.761, p < .001), but no significance was found for germane cognitive load (F = .204, p < .653).

span.label: High- and low-prior-knowledge learners differed significantly in intrinsic and germane cognitive load but not at all in extraneous cognitive load.
span.quote: There were significant differences between high- and low-prior knowledge learners in terms of intrinsic (F = 22.424, p < .000) and germane cognitive load (F = 18.417, p < .000), but no significance was found between high- and low-prior knowledge learners for extraneous cognitive load (F = .018, p = .895)

span.label: Intrinsic cognitive load correlated positively with anxiety and with perceived challenge, and negatively with perceived probability of success.
span.quote: It was found intrinsic cognitive load was positively correlated with anxiety (r = .324, p < .01) and challenge (r = .221, p < .01), but negatively correlated with probability of success (r = -.299, p < .01)

span.label: Prior knowledge and worked-example type interacted significantly on germane cognitive load, though not on intrinsic or extraneous load.
span.quote: However, a significant interaction by germane cognitive load (F1, 107 = 4.72, p < .05, ŋ2 = .04) was found between prior knowledge and worked example

span.label: intrinsic cognitive load
span.quote: Intrinsic cognitive load is defined by the difficulty of the instructional materials that cannot be changed or altered.

span.label: extraneous cognitive load
span.quote: Extraneous cognitive load refers to the mental load caused by improper instructional design like imposing redundant information in learning materials that requires learners’ additional processing effort.

span.label: germane cognitive load
span.quote: It is the mental load induced by the efforts to construct new knowledge or build new schema (Sweller et al., 1998).

span.label: expertise reversal effect
span.quote: That is, the outcome of an instructional strategy is subject to the level of domain prior knowledge of the learner.

span.label: task difficulty
span.quote: Task difficulty refers to the task requirements defined by the level of content difficulty and associative cognitive demands.

span.label: completion-worked example
span.quote: Completion-worked example provides partial solution steps and expect the learners to finish the rest of the problem based on partial solution.

span.label: tri-split method
span.quote: In contrast to median split method, Liu and Reed (1994) proposed a tri-split method that divided the participants into upper-third quarter, lower-third quarter and middle-third quarter.

span.label: production/solution step method (operationalising difficulty)
span.quote: The task difficulty is defined based on Sweller’s (1988) production/solution step method.

span.label: worked example (full- vs. completion-worked)
span.quote: a three-way interaction study was conducted with worked example (full- vs. completion-worked examples), task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) and prior knowledge (high vs. low) serving as independent variables, and cognitive load and performance as dependent variables.

span.label: task difficulty (easy vs. difficult)
span.quote: a three-way interaction study was conducted with worked example (full- vs. completion-worked examples), task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) and prior knowledge (high vs. low) serving as independent variables, and cognitive load and performance as dependent variables.

span.label: domain prior knowledge (high vs. low)
span.quote: a three-way interaction study was conducted with worked example (full- vs. completion-worked examples), task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) and prior knowledge (high vs. low) serving as independent variables, and cognitive load and performance as dependent variables.

span.label: cognitive load (intrinsic, extraneous, germane)
span.quote: a three-way interaction study was conducted with worked example (full- vs. completion-worked examples), task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) and prior knowledge (high vs. low) serving as independent variables, and cognitive load and performance as dependent variables.

span.label: performance (posttest achievement)
span.quote: a three-way interaction study was conducted with worked example (full- vs. completion-worked examples), task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) and prior knowledge (high vs. low) serving as independent variables, and cognitive load and performance as dependent variables.

span.label: One hundred and sixty — Number of participants recruited for the study
span.quote: One hundred and sixty participants were recruited from a Research I university in the western United States.

span.label: F1, 107 = 4.61, p < .05, ŋ2 = .04 — F-statistic, p-value and effect size for the three-way interaction on posttest performance
span.quote: There was a significant three-way between-subjects effects by posttest (F1, 107 = 4.61, p < .05, ŋ2 = .04) (Figure 2), but no significant three-way interaction for types of cognitive load was detected.

span.label: r = .264, p < .01 — Correlation between germane cognitive load and interest
span.quote: The results showed that germane cognitive load was significantly positively correlated with interest (r = .264, p < .01) suggesting the connection between germane cognitive load and learners’ interest in learning.

span.label: r = -.264, p < .01 — Correlation between extraneous and germane cognitive load
span.quote: A negative correlation between extraneous cognitive load and germane cognitive load (r = -.264, p < .01) was detected which confirms Sweller et al.’s (1998) hypothesis about the negative relationship between extraneous and germane cognitive load.

span.label: n = 55, m = 10.564, SD = 1.808 — Size and pretest mean/SD of the high-prior-knowledge group after the split (low group was n = 60, m = 3.458)
span.quote: Based on the results of pretest, the participants were divided into high, low, and middle prior-knowledge levels with one-standard deviation above the mean as high-prior knowledge (n = 55, m = 10.564, SD = 1.808) and one-standard deviation below the mean as low-prior knowledge (n = 60, m = 3.458, SD = 1.808).

span.label: t(1,26) = 1.98, p = .05, 2-tailed — Test statistic for low-prior-knowledge learners doing better on the posttest with full- than completion-worked examples
span.quote: Lower-prior knowledge learners performed better on the posttest with full-worked examples than completion-worked examples (t(1,26) = 1.98, p = .05, 2-tailed).

span.label: Cronbach’s Alpha = .89 — Item reliability of the final algebra problem set in the pilot study
span.quote: A pilot study was run with the final problems reporting a high item reliability of Cronbach’s Alpha = .89.

span.label: 23.25 — Mean age of the participants, with a standard deviation of 6.01
span.quote: The average age of participants was 23.25 with a standard deviation of 6.01.
